opus-5.5.text:
I think it's changing things in a pretty fundamental way, and honestly I don't think we've fully figured it out yet.

The first thing is just volume. A few years ago, the bottleneck in an open-source project was contributors: you had more ideas and more issues than people willing to write code. Now, with coding agents, writing a patch is cheap. Someone can point an agent at an issue and get a plausible-looking PR in twenty minutes. So the number of PRs coming in has gone up a lot, but the number of people who can deeply review them, who really understand the scheduler, the memory management, the kernel paths, hasn't grown at the same rate. The bottleneck has shifted from writing code to reviewing code, and really to judgment.

The second thing is that the quality signal got noisier. Before, if someone sent a large, well-structured PR, that usually meant they had invested a lot of time and understood the system. Now a large, well-formatted PR tells you much less. It might be great, or it might be locally correct but wrong for the architecture: duplicating an abstraction we already have, or adding a special case that makes the next ten features harder. Agents are very good at making things work and much less good at knowing what the project should look like in two years. So as maintainers we have to be clearer about design principles, write them down, and be willing to say no more often.

So a lot of what I think about now is infrastructure for the community, not just for the code. Better CI, so correctness is checked by machines rather than humans. Clearer contribution guidelines, including expectations around AI-generated code: you're responsible for what you submit, you should understand it, and you should be able to answer questions about it. And making the codebase itself more agent-friendly, with clean module boundaries, good docs, and good tests, because if agents are going to be contributors, the codebase is effectively their onboarding material.

There's also a positive side that I don't want to understate. Agents lower the barrier for people to make their first contribution. Someone who knows their hardware or model really well but isn't a deep PyTorch or CUDA expert can now actually get something working and upstream it. For a project like vLLM, which has to support so many models and so many accelerators, that's huge. A lot of the long tail of support can be handled this way.

So my summary would be: the core skill of running a large open-source community is moving from "how do we get enough people to write code" toward "how do we maintain taste and architectural coherence when code is abundant." The scarce resource is now people with good judgment who are willing to spend time reviewing, mentoring, and saying "this works, but it's not the right way." Growing that group of people is, I think, the most important thing for the project right now.

r001.rationale: The response says the scarce skill is judgment: maintaining architectural coherence, deciding when to say no, and choosing which contributions fit the project as code becomes abundant.

r002.rationale: It does not mention résumé-driven junk contributions or any loss of maintainers’ assumption of good faith.

r003.rationale: It does not identify institutional affiliation as a trust signal.

r004.rationale: It does not predict that institutions or major contributors will gain control over project direction.

r005.rationale: It does not argue that maintainers may prefer regenerating a change with an agent over reviewing an outside pull request.

r006.rationale: It discusses contributors using agents to get code working and upstream it, but does not describe users reporting needs while maintainers produce the code.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, this is something I think about almost every day now, because it's changing the job faster than I expected.

The most visible change is volume. A year or two ago, the bottleneck in vLLM was that not enough people could write a good PR. You needed to understand CUDA, PagedAttention, the scheduler, the model loading path. That was a high bar, so the number of contributions was naturally limited by the number of people who had climbed it. Now, with coding agents, the bar to produce a PR that compiles and passes a few tests has dropped dramatically. So we get many more PRs, and many of them look polished on the surface. The bottleneck has shifted from writing code to reviewing code.

And reviewing is actually harder than it used to be, because the signal we relied on is gone. Before, if someone wrote a clean PR with good variable names and a clear description, that was a strong hint they understood the problem. Agents produce that style for free. So a maintainer can no longer judge from the shape of the PR whether the author understands why the change is correct. You have to actually dig in. Sometimes you ask a question in review and the answer comes back and you can tell the person just pasted your comment into the agent and pasted the output back. That's a new failure mode for a community.

So the first thing managing the community now requires is being explicit about what we want from a contributor. It's not "give us code." It's "give us understanding." We've started asking people to explain the design decision in their own words, to describe what they tested and why, to say which alternatives they considered. If an agent helped, that's fine, we use them too, but you need to own the result. A PR is a conversation, not a file drop.

The second thing is that we have to invest much more in automation on our side. If contributions scale up by ten times, human review cannot scale up by ten times. So CI has to catch more, benchmarks have to be automatic, we need better tooling to flag when a change touches a hot path or changes numerics. In a sense, we need our own agents to help triage the agents on the other side. I think the maintainer role is becoming closer to designing the review system than doing every review by hand.

The third change is more subtle, and it's about how knowledge spreads. Historically, a big part of how vLLM grew was people reading the codebase, struggling with it, and gradually becoming experts who could then help others. If people now get answers from an agent instead of from the code or from the community, the pipeline of new maintainers might get thinner. You get many contributors but fewer people who deeply understand the system. That worries me more than the PR volume. So we're trying to be deliberate about documentation, design docs, and making the architecture legible, both for humans and for the agents reading it, because now the agent is also a reader of our docs, and if the docs are wrong, the agent will confidently produce wrong code.

There's a positive side too, and I don't want to sound negative. Agents are great at the long tail. Adding support for one more model architecture, fixing a typo in a config path, porting a kernel to a slightly different shape. Those used to sit in the backlog for months because no one had time. Now a contributor with an agent can clear them in an afternoon, and if the test coverage is good, we can accept them with confidence. So the project is moving faster on breadth, and maintainers can spend their attention on the hard decisions: scheduler design, memory management, how to support new hardware.

So if I summarize, I'd say coding agents turn community management from a people-scaling problem into a trust-and-verification problem. The question is no longer "how do we get more hands," it's "how do we know what's correct, and how do we grow people who can tell." The projects that figure out the second part will be the ones that stay healthy.

r001.rationale: The response says the main bottleneck has shifted to reviewing and verifying code, but does not identify choosing which contributions are worth pursuing as the central challenge.

r002.rationale: It describes a new failure mode where contributors may paste agent output, but does not mention résumé-driven junk contributions or lost trust in participants’ good faith.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify institutional affiliation as a trust signal.

r004.rationale: It predicts changes to review and contributor development, but says nothing about institutions or major contributors gaining control over project direction.

r005.rationale: The response calls review harder and proposes more automation; it does not argue that maintainers should regenerate proposed changes instead of reviewing outside pull requests.

r006.rationale: It asks contributors to explain and own their changes, but does not propose a division of labor where users describe needs and maintainers write the code.

astra-6.text:
I think coding agents shift the bottleneck from writing code to deciding what code should be accepted. They make it easier for people to contribute, which is exciting, but a large open-source community still has to review those contributions and maintain them afterward.

For a project like vLLM, a change can look reasonable locally and still have consequences for performance or compatibility elsewhere. So as contributions become easier to produce, clear tests, benchmarks, and review expectations become more important. Contributors need to explain what problem they’re solving and provide evidence that the change works.

The management challenge is keeping that process welcoming without overwhelming maintainers. Agents can help with implementation and some review work, but someone still needs to understand the tradeoffs and take responsibility for the result. I think that judgment—and helping new contributors develop it—becomes a bigger part of running the community.

r002.rationale: It does not mention résumé-driven junk contributions or a loss of trust in participants’ good faith.

r003.rationale: It does not identify institutional affiliation as a signal for evaluating contributions.

r004.rationale: It does not predict that project direction or control will shift toward institutions and major contributors.

r005.rationale: It says agents can help with implementation and review, but does not argue that maintainers may prefer regenerating a change over reviewing an outside pull request.

r006.rationale: It does not describe users specifying problems or features while maintainers produce the code.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coding agents make writing code easier, but they make deciding what should be merged even more important. In a project like vLLM, a change can look reasonable locally and still affect performance, compatibility, or maintenance somewhere else. So more contributions don’t automatically mean more progress. Review capacity and maintainer attention become the bottleneck.

That changes how you manage the community. You need clear contribution guidelines, good tests, reproducible benchmarks, and a clear sense of who owns each part of the system. You also want contributors to explain the problem they’re solving and provide evidence that their change works. Generating a patch is only one part of contributing; taking responsibility for it matters just as much.

The opportunity is that agents can help people get involved who previously would have struggled to navigate a large codebase. But you still need to help those people develop judgment. I think the maintainer’s role shifts toward setting direction, making tradeoffs explicit, and helping contributors become people you can trust with increasingly difficult decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says coding is easier while deciding what should be merged becomes more important, and that review capacity is the bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It does not mention résumé-driven junk contributions or a loss of trust in participants’ good faith.

r003.rationale: It does not identify institutional affiliation as a trust signal.

r004.rationale: It does not predict that control over project direction will shift toward institutions or major contributors.

r005.rationale: It does not suggest regenerating proposed changes with an agent instead of reviewing outside pull requests.

r006.rationale: It discusses contributors explaining problems and producing changes, but does not envision users describing needs while maintainers produce the code.
